newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Saudi barley buys buoy Australian traders.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Saudi barley buys buoy Australian traders.

text.p: A rush of near-term Australian barley sales to the Middle East has left some traders celebrating favourably-priced deals and others regretting sales at lower prices, grains traders said on Thursday.

Exporters from the state of New South Wales (NSW) are buoyed by recent sales and further inquiries, while grains officials from some other states refuse to comment on recent export deals. After striking a deal last week to sell 90,000 tonnes of feed barley to Saudi Arabia at US$133 a tonne fob, the NSW Grains Board received a further bid on Wednesday night for 30,000 tonnes at $133 a tonne fob, traders said.
"We're feeling pretty good," one NSW grains source said.
The latest bid, from a European trading house for Middle East shipment in the first week of December, confirmed the rising international barley market price, traders said.
The final market in last night's bid is believed to be Saudi Arabia, traders said.
The matter would be under consideration at the NSW Grains Board on Thursday, they said.
This indicated that a recent sale of 30,000 tonnes of feed barley to Saudi Arabia at $130 a tonne by the Australian Barley Board (ABB) was less than favourably priced for growers, they said.
"That really (annoyed) the growers in South Australia, didn't it?", one trader said.
Michael Iwaniw, ABB general manager, would not confirm or deny the sale when contacted by Reuters.
"Whatever business we do is between us and the buyer, it's not up to us to confirm or not, we're doing business deals all the time," he said.
Other traders contacted by Reuters, however, confirmed the sale.
The ABB markets South Australian and Victorian barley.
Queensland had also recently entered into a sale for 50,000 tonnes at $128 a tonne to Saudi Arabia for near-term delivery, traders said.
Marketing agent GrainCo confirmed the sale for Reuters. The shipment leaves Brisbane on Thursday on the Sonic Youth.
Earlier Australian sales mis-judged the market, traders said. Barley was not as plentiful nor as low-priced as exporters perceived, they said.
The present world price could be taken as the $133 bid received last night by the NSW Grains Board, with the present market centring around early deliveries, traders said.
Canada's present poor winter weather was helping southern hemisphere growers and exporters, Robert Thompson, general manager marketing of the NSW Grains Board, said.
With Saudi Arabia's current tender due to expire December 15, Australian traders expect further Saudi inquiries in coming weeks for deliveries early next year, traders said.
